title: The World Philip K. Dick Made (UMI Dissertation #9931275)
author: Pamela Jackson

page_summary:
Pamela Jackson's UC Berkeley doctoral dissertation The World Philip K. Dick Made (UMI Dissertation #9931275, August 1999, 207 pp) is the foundational academic engagement with the Exegesis manuscript and the precursor to the 2011 Lethem/Jackson published edition. At the time of writing, the manuscript was effectively unpublished — Lawrence Sutin had compiled the In Pursuit of VALIS selections (1991), but the full ~8,000-page document was accessible only via the CSU Fullerton Special Collections holdings. Jackson was the first scholar to sustained-read the manuscript at archive, and her dissertation is the document that defined what the 2011 published edition would aim at: chronological-with-thematic-threading selection, generous primary text with conservative interpretive overlay, attention to the recurring concerns (the AI Voice, Zebra, the Black Iron Prison, two-source cosmology) that organize the manuscript despite its non-linear surface.

Method: archival close reading at CSU Fullerton across the available manuscript folders. Where Sutin's 1991 selection had concentrated on selected highlights, Jackson's dissertation reads the full document and tracks recurring concerns and thematic threads across its multi-year span. The dissertation predates the 2011 publication by twelve years, and the 2011 edition's editorial method is in many ways the dissertation's program made institutional.

Contributions to PKD studies: (1) the foundational sustained academic reading of the full Exegesis manuscript, on which all subsequent published-Exegesis scholarship rests; (2) the editorial method (chronological-thematic threading, conservative selection) that shaped the 2011 edition; (3) the archive-mapping work that documented what the CSU Fullerton holdings contain — including manuscript material the published edition leaves out; (4) the academic-credentialing of the Exegesis as a unified late work warranting close-reading attention rather than as scattered fragments.

Position in the literature: Jackson's dissertation is the textual-scholarly foundation of post-2011 Dick studies. Where Sutin established the biographical baseline (1989) and Robinson the novelistic-critical baseline (1984), Jackson established the Exegesis-textual baseline (1999). The 2011 Lethem/Jackson edition is the institutional consolidation of her dissertation's program; subsequent academic engagement with the Exegesis (Davis, Critchley, McKee, Hayles as annotators, and the Dunst-Schlensag 2015 collection generally) builds on the textual ground Jackson laid.

Fan reception: the dissertation is most familiar to academic readers but has been cited in fan venues (Total Dick-Head, PKD Otaku) as the indispensable archival precedent for any current Exegesis study.

Caveats: the PDF in this archive is a scanned image with no extractable text, so full-text search against this document is not currently possible. Citations in subsequent scholarship typically reference Jackson 1999 or the dissertation's UMI number rather than page numbers, given accessibility difficulty.
